title: Comfort, Mobility & Daily Care
html:
Basic care supports comfort, function, dignity, and prevention of secondary harm. The RN individualizes assistance instead of doing everything for the client or assuming independence.

Protect function

  • Encourage the safest level of participation in hygiene, mobility, eating, and elimination.
  • Use positioning and assistive equipment to reduce falls, pressure, aspiration, and injury.
  • Balance activity with rest, then reassess tolerance.
Before oral intake
When swallowing safety is uncertain, pause intake and assess according to the care plan and facility process. Upright positioning reduces risk but does not replace evaluation.

Treat pain as multidimensional

Assess location, quality, severity, timing, function, and the client's goals. Combine ordered pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic measures when appropriate, then evaluate both relief and adverse effects.

Prevent pressure injury

Inspect risk areas, manage moisture, support nutrition and mobility, offload pressure, and reposition based on the client's condition and plan. Document skin findings and response rather than only task completion.

Learning goals

Match assistance to ability, recognize intolerance during routine care, and evaluate comfort without sacrificing safety. This lesson introduces daily-care decisions; Lessons 9–13 develop wound, feeding, elimination, respiratory, and pain care in more depth.

Before a transfer

Check current activity and weight-bearing orders, alertness, pain, strength, balance, symptoms on sitting, and attached devices. Confirm the required equipment and trained assistance. A client who cannot bear weight may need a mechanical lift rather than a one-person pivot. Lock transfer surfaces, clear the route, and use suitable footwear. A gait belt is an aid for an appropriate client, not a substitute for adequate staffing or a lift.

If dizziness or weakness develops, stop and help the client to a supported sitting or lying position; assess and obtain help. Do not insist on finishing the walk. Record symptoms and response so the next caregiver can adjust the plan.

Make daily care collaborative

Ask about preferred routines and privacy. Let a stable client wash the areas they can reach, while helping with fatigue or restricted movement. Refusal calls for exploring pain, embarrassment, beliefs, or timing and offering alternatives, not labeling the client uncooperative. Cleanse gently, dry skin folds, provide oral care, and inspect skin during care. Report new skin changes using objective descriptions.

Worked example

A client can wash their face but becomes breathless while standing at the sink. Stop the activity and assess breathing, symptoms, and vital signs. After the immediate concern is addressed, consider seated care, shorter tasks, rest periods, and the assistance plan. Success means safe participation and acceptable symptom recovery, not merely a completed bath.

Self-check

Before asking “Did the task get done?”, ask “What could this client safely do, what changed during care, and what did I reassess?”

Sources for review

  • Open RN: Mobility, Nursing Fundamentals 2e

Original educational synthesis. Local protocols and qualified faculty guide clinical application.
